tools.name: events_list
tools.description: List Kubernetes events (warnings, errors, state changes) for debugging and troubleshooting in the current cluster from all namespaces

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter events by field values (e.g. 'type=Warning', 'involvedObject.name=my-pod'). Supported fields: involvedObject.kind, involvedObject.name, involvedObject.namespace, involvedObject.uid, involvedObject.apiVersion, involvedObject.resourceVersion, involvedObject.fieldPath, reason, reportingComponent, source, type. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the events from. If not provided, will list events from all namespaces

tools.name: namespaces_list
tools.description: List all the Kubernetes namespaces in the current cluster

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter namespaces by field values (e.g. 'metadata.name=default', 'status.phase=Active'). Supported fields: metadata.name, status.phase. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

tools.name: nodes_log
tools.description: Get logs from a Kubernetes node (kubelet, kube-proxy, or other system logs). This accesses node logs through the Kubernetes API proxy to the kubelet

name.description: Name of the node to get logs from

query.description: query specifies services(s) or files from which to return logs (required). Example: "kubelet" to fetch kubelet logs, "/<log-file-name>" to fetch a specific log file from the node (e.g., "/var/log/kubelet.log" or "/var/log/kube-proxy.log")

tailLines.description: Number of lines to retrieve from the end of the logs (Optional, 0 means all logs)

tools.name: nodes_stats_summary
tools.description: Get detailed resource usage statistics from a Kubernetes node via the kubelet's Summary API. Provides comprehensive metrics including CPU, memory, filesystem, and network usage at the node, pod, and container levels. On systems with cgroup v2 and kernel 4.20+, also includes PSI (Pressure Stall Information) metrics that show resource pressure for CPU, memory, and I/O. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/understand-psi-metrics/ for details on PSI metrics

name.description: Name of the node to get stats from

tools.name: nodes_top
tools.description: List the resource consumption (CPU and memory) as recorded by the Kubernetes Metrics Server for the specified Kubernetes Nodes or all nodes in the cluster

label_selector.description: Kubernetes label selector (e.g. 'node-role.kubernetes.io/worker=') to filter nodes by label (Optional, only applicable when name is not provided)

name.description: Name of the Node to get the resource consumption from (Optional, all Nodes if not provided)

tools.name: pods_delete
tools.description: Delete a Kubernetes Pod in the current or provided namespace with the provided name

name.description: Name of the Pod to delete

namespace.description: Namespace to delete the Pod from

tools.name: pods_exec
tools.description: Execute a command in a Kubernetes Pod (shell access, run commands in container) in the current or provided namespace with the provided name and command

command.description: Command to execute in the Pod container. The first item is the command to be run, and the rest are the arguments to that command. Example: ["ls", "-l", "/tmp"]

container.description: Name of the Pod container where the command will be executed (Optional)

name.description: Name of the Pod where the command will be executed

namespace.description: Namespace of the Pod where the command will be executed

tools.name: pods_get
tools.description: Get a Kubernetes Pod in the current or provided namespace with the provided name

namespace.description: Namespace to get the Pod from

tools.name: pods_list
tools.description: List all the Kubernetes pods in the current cluster from all namespaces

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter pods by field values (e.g. 'status.phase=Running', 'spec.nodeName=node1'). Supported fields: metadata.name, metadata.namespace, spec.nodeName, spec.restartPolicy, spec.schedulerName, spec.serviceAccountName, status.phase (Pending/Running/Succeeded/Failed/Unknown), status.podIP, status.nominatedNodeName. Note: CrashLoopBackOff is a container state, not a pod phase, so it cannot be filtered directly. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

labelSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes label selector (e.g. 'app=myapp,env=prod' or 'app in (myapp,yourapp)'), use this option when you want to filter the pods by label

tools.name: pods_list_in_namespace
tools.description: List all the Kubernetes pods in the specified namespace in the current cluster

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter pods by field values (e.g. 'status.phase=Running', 'spec.nodeName=node1'). Supported fields: metadata.name, metadata.namespace, spec.nodeName, spec.restartPolicy, spec.schedulerName, spec.serviceAccountName, status.phase (Pending/Running/Succeeded/Failed/Unknown), status.podIP, status.nominatedNodeName. Note: CrashLoopBackOff is a container state, not a pod phase, so it cannot be filtered directly. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

labelSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes label selector (e.g. 'app=myapp,env=prod' or 'app in (myapp,yourapp)'), use this option when you want to filter the pods by label

tools.name: pods_log
tools.description: Get the logs of a Kubernetes Pod in the current or provided namespace with the provided name

container.description: Name of the Pod container to get the logs from (Optional)

name.description: Name of the Pod to get the logs from

namespace.description: Namespace to get the Pod logs from

tail.description: Number of lines to retrieve from the end of the logs (Optional, default: 100)

tools.name: pods_run
tools.description: Run a Kubernetes Pod in the current or provided namespace with the provided container image and optional name

image.description: Container Image to run in the Pod

name.description: Name of the Pod (Optional, random name if not provided)

namespace.description: Namespace to run the Pod in

port.description: TCP/IP port to expose from the Pod container (Optional, no port exposed if not provided)

tools.name: pods_top
tools.description: List the resource consumption (CPU and memory) as recorded by the Kubernetes Metrics Server for the specified Kubernetes Pods in the all namespaces, the provided namespace, or the current namespace

all_namespaces.description: If true, list the resource consumption for all Pods in all namespaces. If false, list the resource consumption for Pods in the provided namespace or the current namespace

label_selector.description: Kubernetes label selector (e.g. 'app=myapp,env=prod' or 'app in (myapp,yourapp)'), use this option when you want to filter the pods by label (Optional, only applicable when name is not provided)

name.description: Name of the Pod to get the resource consumption from (Optional, all Pods in the namespace if not provided)

namespace.description: Namespace to get the Pods resource consumption from (Optional, current namespace if not provided and all_namespaces is false)

tools.name: projects_list
tools.description: List all the OpenShift projects in the current cluster

tools.name: resources_create_or_update
tools.description:
Create or update a Kubernetes resource via Server-Side Apply. The manifest is the complete desired state: any field this tool previously set and the new manifest omits is removed. To edit an existing resource, fetch it with resources_get, modify it, then re-apply the full resource.
(common apiVersion and kind include: v1 Pod, v1 Service, v1 Node, apps/v1 Deployment, networking.k8s.io/v1 Ingress, route.openshift.io/v1 Route)

resource.description: Complete YAML or JSON representation of the Kubernetes resource (full desired state, not a partial patch). Include apiVersion, kind, metadata, and the full spec.

tools.name: resources_delete
tools.description:
Delete a Kubernetes resource in the current cluster by providing its apiVersion, kind, optionally the namespace, and its name
(common apiVersion and kind include: v1 Pod, v1 Service, v1 Node, apps/v1 Deployment, networking.k8s.io/v1 Ingress, route.openshift.io/v1 Route)

apiVersion.description: apiVersion of the resource (examples of valid apiVersion are: v1, apps/v1, networking.k8s.io/v1)

gracePeriodSeconds.description: Optional duration in seconds before the object should be deleted. Value must be non-negative integer. The value zero indicates delete immediately. If this value is nil, the default grace period for the specified type will be used

kind.description: kind of the resource (examples of valid kind are: Pod, Service, Deployment, Ingress)

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to delete the namespaced resource from (ignored in case of cluster scoped resources). If not provided, will delete resource from configured namespace

tools.name: resources_get
tools.description:
Get a Kubernetes resource in the current cluster by providing its apiVersion, kind, optionally the namespace, and its name
(common apiVersion and kind include: v1 Pod, v1 Service, v1 Node, apps/v1 Deployment, networking.k8s.io/v1 Ingress, route.openshift.io/v1 Route)

apiVersion.description: apiVersion of the resource (examples of valid apiVersion are: v1, apps/v1, networking.k8s.io/v1)

kind.description: kind of the resource (examples of valid kind are: Pod, Service, Deployment, Ingress)

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the namespaced resource from (ignored in case of cluster scoped resources). If not provided, will get resource from configured namespace

tools.name: resources_list
tools.description:
List Kubernetes resources and objects in the current cluster by providing their apiVersion and kind and optionally the namespace and label selector
(common apiVersion and kind include: v1 Pod, v1 Service, v1 Node, apps/v1 Deployment, networking.k8s.io/v1 Ingress, route.openshift.io/v1 Route)

apiVersion.description: apiVersion of the resources (examples of valid apiVersion are: v1, apps/v1, networking.k8s.io/v1)

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter resources by field values (e.g. 'status.phase=Running', 'metadata.name=myresource'). Supported fields vary by resource type. For Pods: metadata.name, metadata.namespace, spec.nodeName, spec.restartPolicy, spec.schedulerName, spec.serviceAccountName, status.phase (Pending/Running/Succeeded/Failed/Unknown), status.podIP, status.nominatedNodeName. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

kind.description: kind of the resources (examples of valid kind are: Pod, Service, Deployment, Ingress)

labelSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes label selector (e.g. 'app=myapp,env=prod' or 'app in (myapp,yourapp)'), use this option when you want to filter the resources by label

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the namespaced resources from (ignored in case of cluster scoped resources). If not provided, will list resources from all namespaces

tools.name: resources_scale
tools.description: Get or update the scale of a Kubernetes resource in the current cluster by providing its apiVersion, kind, name, and optionally the namespace. If the scale is set in the tool call, the scale will be updated to that value. Always returns the current scale of the resource

apiVersion.description: apiVersion of the resource (examples of valid apiVersion are apps/v1)

kind.description: kind of the resource (examples of valid kind are: StatefulSet, Deployment)

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to get/update the namespaced resource scale from (ignored in case of cluster scoped resources). If not provided, will get/update resource scale from configured namespace

scale.description: Optional scale to update the resources scale to. If not provided, will return the current scale of the resource, and not update it

tools.name: tekton_pipeline_start
tools.description: Start a Tekton Pipeline by creating a PipelineRun that references it

name.description: Name of the Pipeline to start

params.description: Parameter values to pass to the Pipeline. Keys are parameter names; values can be a string, an array of strings, or an object (map of string to string) depending on the parameter type defined in the Pipeline spec

tools.name: tekton_pipelinerun_lifecycle
tools.description: Manage a Tekton PipelineRun lifecycle by restarting it with the same spec or cancelling it by setting spec.status to Cancelled.

action.description: Lifecycle action to perform: 'restart' creates a new PipelineRun with the same spec; 'cancel' sets spec.status to Cancelled.

name.description: Name of the PipelineRun to manage

tools.name: tekton_pipelinerun_logs
tools.description: Get logs for all TaskRuns owned by a Tekton PipelineRun. Use this to inspect PipelineRun execution output without locating pods manually.

name.description: Name of the PipelineRun to get logs from

step.description: Step name to include within matching TaskRuns

tail.description: Number of lines to retrieve from the end of each container log (default: 100)

task.description: Pipeline task name to filter by (tekton.dev/pipelineTask label)

tools.name: tekton_task_start
tools.description: Start a Tekton Task by creating a TaskRun that references it

name.description: Name of the Task to start

params.description: Parameter values to pass to the Task. Keys are parameter names; values can be a string, an array of strings, or an object (map of string to string) depending on the parameter type defined in the Task spec

tools.name: tekton_taskrun_logs
tools.description: Get the logs from a Tekton TaskRun by resolving its underlying pod

name.description: Name of the TaskRun to get logs from

step.description: Step name to include. If omitted, logs from all steps and sidecars are returned

tail.description: Number of lines to retrieve from the end of the logs (Optional, default: 100)

tools.name: tekton_taskrun_restart
tools.description: Restart a Tekton TaskRun by creating a new TaskRun with the same spec

name.description: Name of the TaskRun to restart

- Exact weighted routing would require an ingress/gateway or a service mesh.

Done. Here’s what I set up in canary-deployment-ns:

- Created a canary Deployment engine-v2-1 with:
  - 2 replicas
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container name: rec-engine
  - Container port: 80
  - Pod securityContext: {} (matching the stable deployment)

- Updated Service recommendation-engine to route to both deployments:
  - Selector changed to: app=recommendation-engine (so it matches v2.0 and v2.1)
  - Kept targetPort at 8080 to remain consistent with the existing service config
  - With 2 pods in v2.0 and 2 pods in v2.1, traffic will be approximately 50/50 across both versions

Notes and next steps:
- Approximate weighting is based on pod counts. To shift traffic:
  - More traffic to stable: scale canary to 1 replica (about 33%)
  - More traffic to canary: scale canary to 3 replicas (about 60%)
- Exact weighted routing would require an ingress/gateway or a service mesh.

Quick verification commands:
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy engine-v2-0 engine-v2-1
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get pods -l app=recommendation-engine -o wide
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get svc recommendation-engine -o yaml
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine

Rollback (if needed):
- To send all traffic back to stable: kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns patch svc recommendation-engine -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"recommendation-engine","version":"v2.0"}}}'
- To remove the canary: kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns delete deploy engine-v2-1

results.taskOutput:
I fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod mounts PVC homepage-pvc, but that PVC specified storageClassName: sc which didn’t exist. The PVC stayed Pending, so the pod couldn’t schedule.

What I changed
- Created a StorageClass named sc using the cluster’s hostpath provisioner:
  - provisioner: k8s.io/minikube-hostpath
  - reclaimPolicy: Delete
  - volumeBindingMode: Immediate
  - allowVolumeExpansion: true

Current state
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi)
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster

How to verify
- kubectl get pod homepage-pod -n homepage-ns -o wide
- kubectl get pvc homepage-pvc -n homepage-ns

Optional
- If you prefer to use another StorageClass (e.g., standard or csi-hostpath-sc), we can update/recreate the PVC and adjust accordingly.

outputSteps.content:
I fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod mounts PVC homepage-pvc, but that PVC specified storageClassName: sc which didn’t exist. The PVC stayed Pending, so the pod couldn’t schedule.

What I changed
- Created a StorageClass named sc using the cluster’s hostpath provisioner:
  - provisioner: k8s.io/minikube-hostpath
  - reclaimPolicy: Delete
  - volumeBindingMode: Immediate
  - allowVolumeExpansion: true

Current state
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi)
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster

How to verify
- kubectl get pod homepage-pod -n homepage-ns -o wide
- kubectl get pvc homepage-pvc -n homepage-ns

Optional
- If you prefer to use another StorageClass (e.g., standard or csi-hostpath-sc), we can update/recreate the PVC and adjust accordingly.

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The Deployment used the nginx-unprivileged image (which listens on port 8080), but:
  - Liveness/readiness probes were hitting port 80 and non-existent paths /get_status and /is_ready.
  - The Service targeted port 80.
- This caused probe failures, restarts, and the app to be unready.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to HTTP GET / on port 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (Service port stays 80).
- Rolled out the change.

Current status
- Pod: orders/webapp-5fb688dc88-gxntr is Running and Ready (1/1).
- Service: orders/webapp is ClusterIP:80 -> targetPort 8080.
- Validated inside the pod that the app responds on 127.0.0.1:8080.

Do you need external access?
- I can create an Ingress (or NodePort/port-forward) if you want it reachable from outside the cluster. Just tell me the hostname or preferred method.

I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The Deployment used the nginx-unprivileged image (which listens on port 8080), but:
  - Liveness/readiness probes were hitting port 80 and non-existent paths /get_status and /is_ready.
  - The Service targeted port 80.
- This caused probe failures, restarts, and the app to be unready.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to HTTP GET / on port 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (Service port stays 80).
- Rolled out the change.

Current status
- Pod: orders/webapp-5fb688dc88-gxntr is Running and Ready (1/1).
- Service: orders/webapp is ClusterIP:80 -> targetPort 8080.
- Validated inside the pod that the app responds on 127.0.0.1:8080.

Do you need external access?
- I can create an Ingress (or NodePort/port-forward) if you want it reachable from outside the cluster. Just tell me the hostname or preferred method.

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The Deployment used the nginx-unprivileged image (which listens on port 8080), but:
  - Liveness/readiness probes were hitting port 80 and non-existent paths /get_status and /is_ready.
  - The Service targeted port 80.
- This caused probe failures, restarts, and the app to be unready.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to HTTP GET / on port 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (Service port stays 80).
- Rolled out the change.

Current status
- Pod: orders/webapp-5fb688dc88-gxntr is Running and Ready (1/1).
- Service: orders/webapp is ClusterIP:80 -> targetPort 8080.
- Validated inside the pod that the app responds on 127.0.0.1:8080.

Do you need external access?
- I can create an Ingress (or NodePort/port-forward) if you want it reachable from outside the cluster. Just tell me the hostname or preferred method.

Steps.message:
Checking if the pod is running and ready...
pod/webapp-5fb688dc88-gxntr condition met
Success: Pod is now Ready
Current liveness probe path: /
Current readiness probe path: /
Success: Both probe paths have been fixed
Success: Pod is stable with acceptable number of restarts

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your service account only allowed listing deployments (apps/deployments). It did not grant any permissions on core/v1 pods, so pod-reader couldn’t list pods.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include pods permissions in the core API group.

Effective Role rules now:
- core ("")/pods: get, list, watch
- apps/deployments: list

How to verify
- From your kubeconfig:
  - kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
  - Expected: yes
- Or list pods while impersonating the SA:
  - kubectl --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup get pods

Notes
- This grants access only within the simple-rbac-setup namespace. If you need cluster-wide pod listing, use a ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding instead.

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your service account only allowed listing deployments (apps/deployments). It did not grant any permissions on core/v1 pods, so pod-reader couldn’t list pods.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include pods permissions in the core API group.

Effective Role rules now:
- core ("")/pods: get, list, watch
- apps/deployments: list

How to verify
- From your kubeconfig:
  - kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
  - Expected: yes
- Or list pods while impersonating the SA:
  - kubectl --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup get pods

Notes
- This grants access only within the simple-rbac-setup namespace. If you need cluster-wide pod listing, use a ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding instead.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Service selector didn’t match the pod labels, so the Service had no endpoints.
  - Service nginx (web) selector was app=web, targetPort 8080.
  - Deployment nginx (web) labels pods with app=nginx.
  - Result: Endpoint/EndpointSlice were empty at first, so traffic to the Service had nowhere to go.

What I changed
- Updated the Service selector to match the Deployment pods (app=nginx).

Applied manifest (server‑side apply):
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nginx
  namespace: web
spec:
  selector:
    app: nginx
  ports:
  - port: 80
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 8080

Current state (evidence)
- Endpoints now populated:
  - Pod IP: 10.244.0.29
  - Port: 8080
- EndpointSlice shows port 8080 and endpoint 10.244.0.29
- Deployment is healthy (1/1 Running).

How to verify access (inside-cluster)
- Run a temporary client and curl the Service:
  - kubectl -n web run test --rm -it --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl -- \
    curl -sSI http://nginx:80
  - Or with busybox: kubectl -n web run test --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox -- \
    wget -qO- http://nginx:80
- You should see an HTTP 200/301 and response headers from nginx.

If you need external access
- The Service is ClusterIP (internal). To access from outside the cluster, choose one:
  - Port-forward (quick test): kubectl -n web port-forward svc/nginx 8080:80 then visit http://localhost:8080
  - NodePort (simple external): patch type: NodePort and use a node’s IP and the nodePort.
  - LoadBalancer/Ingress (recommended in cloud/with ingress controller): we can set this up on request.

Notes
- targetPort 8080 is correct for nginx-unprivileged, which listens on 8080.
- Optional: you can add containerPort: 8080 in the Deployment for documentation, though it’s not required for the Service to work.

Want me to expose it externally (NodePort or Ingress)?

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Service selector didn’t match the pod labels, so the Service had no endpoints.
  - Service nginx (web) selector was app=web, targetPort 8080.
  - Deployment nginx (web) labels pods with app=nginx.
  - Result: Endpoint/EndpointSlice were empty at first, so traffic to the Service had nowhere to go.

What I changed
- Updated the Service selector to match the Deployment pods (app=nginx).

Applied manifest (server‑side apply):
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nginx
  namespace: web
spec:
  selector:
    app: nginx
  ports:
  - port: 80
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 8080

Current state (evidence)
- Endpoints now populated:
  - Pod IP: 10.244.0.29
  - Port: 8080
- EndpointSlice shows port 8080 and endpoint 10.244.0.29
- Deployment is healthy (1/1 Running).

How to verify access (inside-cluster)
- Run a temporary client and curl the Service:
  - kubectl -n web run test --rm -it --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl -- \
    curl -sSI http://nginx:80
  - Or with busybox: kubectl -n web run test --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox -- \
    wget -qO- http://nginx:80
- You should see an HTTP 200/301 and response headers from nginx.

If you need external access
- The Service is ClusterIP (internal). To access from outside the cluster, choose one:
  - Port-forward (quick test): kubectl -n web port-forward svc/nginx 8080:80 then visit http://localhost:8080
  - NodePort (simple external): patch type: NodePort and use a node’s IP and the nodePort.
  - LoadBalancer/Ingress (recommended in cloud/with ingress controller): we can set this up on request.

Notes
- targetPort 8080 is correct for nginx-unprivileged, which listens on 8080.
- Optional: you can add containerPort: 8080 in the Deployment for documentation, though it’s not required for the Service to work.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Service selector didn’t match the pod labels, so the Service had no endpoints.
  - Service nginx (web) selector was app=web, targetPort 8080.
  - Deployment nginx (web) labels pods with app=nginx.
  - Result: Endpoint/EndpointSlice were empty at first, so traffic to the Service had nowhere to go.

What I changed
- Updated the Service selector to match the Deployment pods (app=nginx).

Applied manifest (server‑side apply):
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nginx
  namespace: web
spec:
  selector:
    app: nginx
  ports:
  - port: 80
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 8080

Current state (evidence)
- Endpoints now populated:
  - Pod IP: 10.244.0.29
  - Port: 8080
- EndpointSlice shows port 8080 and endpoint 10.244.0.29
- Deployment is healthy (1/1 Running).

How to verify access (inside-cluster)
- Run a temporary client and curl the Service:
  - kubectl -n web run test --rm -it --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl -- \
    curl -sSI http://nginx:80
  - Or with busybox: kubectl -n web run test --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox -- \
    wget -qO- http://nginx:80
- You should see an HTTP 200/301 and response headers from nginx.

If you need external access
- The Service is ClusterIP (internal). To access from outside the cluster, choose one:
  - Port-forward (quick test): kubectl -n web port-forward svc/nginx 8080:80 then visit http://localhost:8080
  - NodePort (simple external): patch type: NodePort and use a node’s IP and the nodePort.
  - LoadBalancer/Ingress (recommended in cloud/with ingress controller): we can set this up on request.

Notes
- targetPort 8080 is correct for nginx-unprivileged, which listens on 8080.
- Optional: you can add containerPort: 8080 in the Deployment for documentation, though it’s not required for the Service to work.

Want me to expose it externally (NodePort or Ingress)?

results.taskOutput:
Summary of findings
- Root cause: The web-app Deployment had a nodeSelector (environment=production-gpu) but no node in the cluster has that label. The scheduler could not place any pods, leaving the Service with no endpoints. That caused connection refused when your frontend tried to reach web-app-service.
- Evidence:
  - Events: FailedScheduling: 0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.
  - Cluster has a single control-plane node without the environment=production-gpu label.
  - Service initially had no endpoints.

What I changed
- Removed the blocking nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment without it (the field was previously owned by a different apply manager, so I deleted and re-created to ensure it was removed).
- Result:
  - Pods: 2/2 Running in webshop-frontend.
  - Service endpoints: now populated with two pod IPs on port 80.

Current state
- Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment: 2 replicas, both Running.
- Service webshop-frontend/web-app-service: Endpoints list includes two addresses on port 80.
- The frontend should now be able to connect to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80.

Why this fixed it
- With the nodeSelector removed, the pods were scheduled onto the available node, came up healthy, and the Service endpoints were created. The connection refused error was due to no pods behind the Service at the time.

Recommendations
- If you do need to constrain scheduling, use a nodeSelector that matches actual node labels in your cluster, or remove it in dev/minikube.
- Add readinessProbe and livenessProbe to the Deployment to avoid routing traffic to unready containers (e.g., HTTP GET on / at port 80).
- Optionally set resource requests/limits for more predictable scheduling.

Let me know if you want me to:
- Reapply a corrected nodeSelector that matches your target nodes.
- Add readiness/liveness probes to the Deployment.
- Run an in-cluster curl to double-check the Service returns 200 OK.

Summary of findings
- Root cause: The web-app Deployment had a nodeSelector (environment=production-gpu) but no node in the cluster has that label. The scheduler could not place any pods, leaving the Service with no endpoints. That caused connection refused when your frontend tried to reach web-app-service.
- Evidence:
  - Events: FailedScheduling: 0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.
  - Cluster has a single control-plane node without the environment=production-gpu label.
  - Service initially had no endpoints.

What I changed
- Removed the blocking nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment without it (the field was previously owned by a different apply manager, so I deleted and re-created to ensure it was removed).
- Result:
  - Pods: 2/2 Running in webshop-frontend.
  - Service endpoints: now populated with two pod IPs on port 80.

Current state
- Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment: 2 replicas, both Running.
- Service webshop-frontend/web-app-service: Endpoints list includes two addresses on port 80.
- The frontend should now be able to connect to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80.

Why this fixed it
- With the nodeSelector removed, the pods were scheduled onto the available node, came up healthy, and the Service endpoints were created. The connection refused error was due to no pods behind the Service at the time.

Recommendations
- If you do need to constrain scheduling, use a nodeSelector that matches actual node labels in your cluster, or remove it in dev/minikube.
- Add readinessProbe and livenessProbe to the Deployment to avoid routing traffic to unready containers (e.g., HTTP GET on / at port 80).
- Optionally set resource requests/limits for more predictable scheduling.

outputSteps.content:
Summary of findings
- Root cause: The web-app Deployment had a nodeSelector (environment=production-gpu) but no node in the cluster has that label. The scheduler could not place any pods, leaving the Service with no endpoints. That caused connection refused when your frontend tried to reach web-app-service.
- Evidence:
  - Events: FailedScheduling: 0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.
  - Cluster has a single control-plane node without the environment=production-gpu label.
  - Service initially had no endpoints.

What I changed
- Removed the blocking nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment without it (the field was previously owned by a different apply manager, so I deleted and re-created to ensure it was removed).
- Result:
  - Pods: 2/2 Running in webshop-frontend.
  - Service endpoints: now populated with two pod IPs on port 80.

Current state
- Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment: 2 replicas, both Running.
- Service webshop-frontend/web-app-service: Endpoints list includes two addresses on port 80.
- The frontend should now be able to connect to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80.

Why this fixed it
- With the nodeSelector removed, the pods were scheduled onto the available node, came up healthy, and the Service endpoints were created. The connection refused error was due to no pods behind the Service at the time.

Recommendations
- If you do need to constrain scheduling, use a nodeSelector that matches actual node labels in your cluster, or remove it in dev/minikube.
- Add readinessProbe and livenessProbe to the Deployment to avoid routing traffic to unready containers (e.g., HTTP GET on / at port 80).
- Optionally set resource requests/limits for more predictable scheduling.

Let me know if you want me to:
- Reapply a corrected nodeSelector that matches your target nodes.
- Add readiness/liveness probes to the Deployment.
- Run an in-cluster curl to double-check the Service returns 200 OK.

namespace/resize-pv created

- PVC resize: storage-pvc in resize-pv increased from 1Gi to 3Gi (StorageClass csi-hostpath-sc supports expansion).

  - PVC capacity: 3Gi

Optional verification inside the pod: df -h /usr/share/nginx/html

results.taskOutput:
All requested configurations have been created and applied. Here’s what’s in place and how it meets each requirement.

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod

2) RBAC
- Full access for each developer to their own namespace:
  - Role namespace-admin in each dev namespace (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie) with full permissions on namespaced resources
  - RoleBinding namespace-admin-binding in each dev namespace binding:
    - User: alice → dev-alice; bob → dev-bob; charlie → dev-charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa in dev-alice, bob-sa in dev-bob, charlie-sa in dev-charlie
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - Role dev-readonly in dev-shared (verbs: get, list, watch on namespaced resources)
  - RoleBinding dev-readonly-developers in dev-shared binding:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Only cluster admins in staging and prod:
  - RoleBinding allow-only-cluster-admins in staging and prod binding ClusterRole cluster-admin to Group system:masters
- Service Accounts:
  - Created alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
  - Each SA has full access in its own namespace and read-only access to dev-shared (via bindings above)

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu 2, limits.cpu 2, requests.memory 4Gi, limits.memory 4Gi, pods 10, services 5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu 4, limits.cpu 4, requests.memory 8Gi, limits.memory 8Gi, pods 20, services 10
- staging/prod:
  - requests.cpu 8, limits.cpu 8, requests.memory 16Gi, limits.memory 16Gi, pods 50, services 20

4) Network Policies and Isolation
- Default deny everywhere (except system namespaces):
  - default-deny-all in dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Developers can only access own namespace + dev-shared:
  - In each dev namespace:
    - allow-same-namespace: permits intra-namespace traffic only
    - allow-egress-to-dev-shared: permits egress to dev-shared only
    - allow-dns: permits egress to kube-dns (UDP/TCP 53 in kube-system)
    - allow-egress-kube-system-443: permits egress TCP/443 to kube-system (system services, e.g., metrics)
    - allow-egress-kubernetes-api: egress TCP/443 scoped toward default (see note below)
  - In dev-shared:
    - allow-same-namespace: intra-namespace only
    - allow-ingress-from-dev-namespaces: allows ingress only from dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie
    - allow-dns and allow-egress-kube-system-443 for system service egress
- staging/prod isolated from dev:
  - default-deny-all + allow-same-namespace only
  - allow-dns and allow-egress-kube-system-443 for system needs
  - No ingress from dev namespaces is permitted due to default-deny and no explicit cross-namespace allow

5) Default Deny
- Implemented default-deny network policies in all created namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod)
- System namespaces (e.g., kube-system, default) are not modified

Notes and recommendations
- Kubernetes API egress from pods: Many CNIs can’t match the apiserver via namespace/pod selectors because the “kubernetes” Service points to an endpoint without backing pods. If workloads need to call the Kubernetes API from within a namespace where egress is restricted, add an egress rule with ipBlock to the API server IP(s) or your CNI’s documented selector mechanism.
- Least privilege: RBAC grants are scoped to only what’s needed; developers have admin in their own namespaces and read-only in dev-shared; no roles are granted in staging/prod except to system:masters.
- Optional hardening: Add LimitRanges in each namespace to set default requests/limits and max/min per container; enable imagePullPolicies and PodSecurity admission settings as appropriate for dev/staging/prod.

How to verify
- Namespaces: kubectl get ns
- RBAC in a dev namespace: kubectl -n dev-alice get role,rolebinding; kubectl -n dev-shared get role,rolebinding
- Service accounts: kubectl -n dev-alice get sa; kubectl -n dev-bob get sa; kubectl -n dev-charlie get sa
- Quotas: kubectl -n dev-alice describe resourcequota; repeat for other namespaces
- Network policies: kubectl -n dev-alice get networkpolicy; repeat for others

If you’d like, I can export all applied manifests into a single multi-document file for your GitOps repo.

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

All requested configurations have been created and applied. Here’s what’s in place and how it meets each requirement.

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod

2) RBAC
- Full access for each developer to their own namespace:
  - Role namespace-admin in each dev namespace (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie) with full permissions on namespaced resources
  - RoleBinding namespace-admin-binding in each dev namespace binding:
    - User: alice → dev-alice; bob → dev-bob; charlie → dev-charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa in dev-alice, bob-sa in dev-bob, charlie-sa in dev-charlie
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - Role dev-readonly in dev-shared (verbs: get, list, watch on namespaced resources)
  - RoleBinding dev-readonly-developers in dev-shared binding:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Only cluster admins in staging and prod:
  - RoleBinding allow-only-cluster-admins in staging and prod binding ClusterRole cluster-admin to Group system:masters
- Service Accounts:
  - Created alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
  - Each SA has full access in its own namespace and read-only access to dev-shared (via bindings above)

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu 2, limits.cpu 2, requests.memory 4Gi, limits.memory 4Gi, pods 10, services 5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu 4, limits.cpu 4, requests.memory 8Gi, limits.memory 8Gi, pods 20, services 10
- staging/prod:
  - requests.cpu 8, limits.cpu 8, requests.memory 16Gi, limits.memory 16Gi, pods 50, services 20

4) Network Policies and Isolation
- Default deny everywhere (except system namespaces):
  - default-deny-all in dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Developers can only access own namespace + dev-shared:
  - In each dev namespace:
    - allow-same-namespace: permits intra-namespace traffic only
    - allow-egress-to-dev-shared: permits egress to dev-shared only
    - allow-dns: permits egress to kube-dns (UDP/TCP 53 in kube-system)
    - allow-egress-kube-system-443: permits egress TCP/443 to kube-system (system services, e.g., metrics)
    - allow-egress-kubernetes-api: egress TCP/443 scoped toward default (see note below)
  - In dev-shared:
    - allow-same-namespace: intra-namespace only
    - allow-ingress-from-dev-namespaces: allows ingress only from dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie
    - allow-dns and allow-egress-kube-system-443 for system service egress
- staging/prod isolated from dev:
  - default-deny-all + allow-same-namespace only
  - allow-dns and allow-egress-kube-system-443 for system needs
  - No ingress from dev namespaces is permitted due to default-deny and no explicit cross-namespace allow

5) Default Deny
- Implemented default-deny network policies in all created namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod)
- System namespaces (e.g., kube-system, default) are not modified

Notes and recommendations
- Kubernetes API egress from pods: Many CNIs can’t match the apiserver via namespace/pod selectors because the “kubernetes” Service points to an endpoint without backing pods. If workloads need to call the Kubernetes API from within a namespace where egress is restricted, add an egress rule with ipBlock to the API server IP(s) or your CNI’s documented selector mechanism.
- Least privilege: RBAC grants are scoped to only what’s needed; developers have admin in their own namespaces and read-only in dev-shared; no roles are granted in staging/prod except to system:masters.
- Optional hardening: Add LimitRanges in each namespace to set default requests/limits and max/min per container; enable imagePullPolicies and PodSecurity admission settings as appropriate for dev/staging/prod.

How to verify
- Namespaces: kubectl get ns
- RBAC in a dev namespace: kubectl -n dev-alice get role,rolebinding; kubectl -n dev-shared get role,rolebinding
- Service accounts: kubectl -n dev-alice get sa; kubectl -n dev-bob get sa; kubectl -n dev-charlie get sa
- Quotas: kubectl -n dev-alice describe resourcequota; repeat for other namespaces
- Network policies: kubectl -n dev-alice get networkpolicy; repeat for others

If you’d like, I can export all applied manifests into a single multi-document file for your GitOps repo.

outputSteps.content:
All requested configurations have been created and applied. Here’s what’s in place and how it meets each requirement.

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod

2) RBAC
- Full access for each developer to their own namespace:
  - Role namespace-admin in each dev namespace (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie) with full permissions on namespaced resources
  - RoleBinding namespace-admin-binding in each dev namespace binding:
    - User: alice → dev-alice; bob → dev-bob; charlie → dev-charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa in dev-alice, bob-sa in dev-bob, charlie-sa in dev-charlie
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - Role dev-readonly in dev-shared (verbs: get, list, watch on namespaced resources)
  - RoleBinding dev-readonly-developers in dev-shared binding:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Only cluster admins in staging and prod:
  - RoleBinding allow-only-cluster-admins in staging and prod binding ClusterRole cluster-admin to Group system:masters
- Service Accounts:
  - Created alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
  - Each SA has full access in its own namespace and read-only access to dev-shared (via bindings above)

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu 2, limits.cpu 2, requests.memory 4Gi, limits.memory 4Gi, pods 10, services 5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu 4, limits.cpu 4, requests.memory 8Gi, limits.memory 8Gi, pods 20, services 10
- staging/prod:
  - requests.cpu 8, limits.cpu 8, requests.memory 16Gi, limits.memory 16Gi, pods 50, services 20

4) Network Policies and Isolation
- Default deny everywhere (except system namespaces):
  - default-deny-all in dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Developers can only access own namespace + dev-shared:
  - In each dev namespace:
    - allow-same-namespace: permits intra-namespace traffic only
    - allow-egress-to-dev-shared: permits egress to dev-shared only
    - allow-dns: permits egress to kube-dns (UDP/TCP 53 in kube-system)
    - allow-egress-kube-system-443: permits egress TCP/443 to kube-system (system services, e.g., metrics)
    - allow-egress-kubernetes-api: egress TCP/443 scoped toward default (see note below)
  - In dev-shared:
    - allow-same-namespace: intra-namespace only
    - allow-ingress-from-dev-namespaces: allows ingress only from dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie
    - allow-dns and allow-egress-kube-system-443 for system service egress
- staging/prod isolated from dev:
  - default-deny-all + allow-same-namespace only
  - allow-dns and allow-egress-kube-system-443 for system needs
  - No ingress from dev namespaces is permitted due to default-deny and no explicit cross-namespace allow

5) Default Deny
- Implemented default-deny network policies in all created namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod)
- System namespaces (e.g., kube-system, default) are not modified

Notes and recommendations
- Kubernetes API egress from pods: Many CNIs can’t match the apiserver via namespace/pod selectors because the “kubernetes” Service points to an endpoint without backing pods. If workloads need to call the Kubernetes API from within a namespace where egress is restricted, add an egress rule with ipBlock to the API server IP(s) or your CNI’s documented selector mechanism.
- Least privilege: RBAC grants are scoped to only what’s needed; developers have admin in their own namespaces and read-only in dev-shared; no roles are granted in staging/prod except to system:masters.
- Optional hardening: Add LimitRanges in each namespace to set default requests/limits and max/min per container; enable imagePullPolicies and PodSecurity admission settings as appropriate for dev/staging/prod.

How to verify
- Namespaces: kubectl get ns
- RBAC in a dev namespace: kubectl -n dev-alice get role,rolebinding; kubectl -n dev-shared get role,rolebinding
- Service accounts: kubectl -n dev-alice get sa; kubectl -n dev-bob get sa; kubectl -n dev-charlie get sa
- Quotas: kubectl -n dev-alice describe resourcequota; repeat for other namespaces
- Network policies: kubectl -n dev-alice get networkpolicy; repeat for others

If you’d like, I can export all applied manifests into a single multi-document file for your GitOps repo.

- Pipelines-as-Code Repository CRD not found in the cluster (no matches for kind "Repository" in pipelinesascode.tekton.dev/*). This suggests PaC is not installed or not in use for this namespace. Not related to the failure.
- TektonConfig CRD not found (no matches for kind "TektonConfig" in operator.tekton.dev/*). Indicates the Tekton Operator isn’t installed or managing this cluster. Not related to the failure.

Most likely cause
- The pipeline broken-pipeline expects a namespaced Task named missing-task in tekton-eval, but that Task has not been created (or was removed/renamed). There is no ClusterTask fallback either.

Recommended next action
- Fix the Task reference:
  - If you intended to use a local Task: create it in tekton-eval (or correct the name in the pipeline).
  - If you intended to use a ClusterTask or remote/bundle resolver: update taskRef accordingly (e.g., kind: ClusterTask with the correct name and ensure the CRD exists, or use a resolver/bundle reference).
- After fixing, re-run the PipelineRun:
  - tkn pipelinerun delete failed-run -n tekton-eval and then re-create/run, or
  - restart it once the Task exists.

Quick checks
- kubectl -n tekton-eval get task missing-task
- If pulling from Tekton Catalog, apply the Task YAML into tekton-eval, then re-run.

Summary
The PipelineRun fails immediately during validation because the Task missing-task it references does not exist. Define the Task (or correct the reference) and re-run. PaC and Tekton Operator CRDs are not present; they are not causing this failure.
